Language learning for beginners: speak, correct, review

Beginner advice often looks like a shopping list. A better strategy is to speak your own sentences, get specific corrections, and review them before you forget.

Published April 26, 2024 · 8 min read · Sławomir Onyszko ·Updated November 14, 2026

Beginner advice often looks like a shopping list: an app, a textbook, a podcast, a flashcard deck, a grammar course. You collect the resources and hope that one of them will work.

The problem is that resources are not a strategy. A strategy is what you do in a session, especially when you learn alone. For a beginner, the simplest useful strategy has three steps: speak, correct, and review.

Start with your reason and a goal that is yours

Before you choose an app, answer why you are learning the language. Do you want to talk at work, travel, read books, or talk to your partner's family? The reason does not have to be big, but it has to be yours.

Fluency means something different to everyone. For one person it is a relaxed conversation about everyday life. For another it is a conversation about work. For someone else it is a longer discussion. Instead of waiting for a huge goal, set small stages: introduce yourself, describe your day, ask a question, answer a question. The stages do not need a date. They need to make sense.

The trap: collecting resources

A new app feels like progress. A new textbook does too. But neither one makes you speak. You speak when you build your own sentence and say it out loud.

This is why beginners often feel busy and still freeze in a real conversation. They have collected words and audio, but they have never built their own sentences from them.

The strategy: speaking, correction, review

Words are the building blocks. Without them, you cannot build a sentence. But a list of words you only recognize does not turn into speaking. You need a few words you can use and one sentence you can say.

The first step is speaking. Pick a few words you know and build your own sentence with them. Then say it out loud. That is the moment when a word becomes a skill, not just a familiar shape on paper.

The second step is correction. A correction tells you what you said, what a more natural version is, and why. Without it, you can repeat the same mistake.

The third step is review. A correction you never return to disappears quickly. Flashcards that make you recall the word before you see the answer, and spaced review, bring words and corrections back when they start to fade.

The three steps are simple. The power is in doing them together. Speaking without correction can repeat a mistake. Correction without review disappears. Review without speaking is only recognition.

Speak from the first session

You do not need to master grammar before you open your mouth. Start with a short answer about something real: your day, your work, a picture, or a story you read.

If you only know a few words, use them. "Trabajo en una tienda. Empiezo a las ocho. Me gusta mi equipo." That is a real answer and something a correction can work with.

At the beginning you do not need long dialogues. 3 sentences of your own are enough. Speaking shows right away whether you really know a word. If you cannot use it, go back to it or replace it with something simpler. That is not a failure. It is a hint.

A correction you can understand

A correction is not a score. It is information. A good correction tells you three things:

  • what you said
  • what a more natural version is
  • why the change matters

Example: "Soy 30 años" becomes "Tengo 30 años". Why? Spanish uses "tener" for age, not "ser". Once you understand the pattern, you can fix more than one sentence.

You can get a correction from a tutor, from a language exchange partner, or from an app that transcribes your answer and shows a corrected version. The explanation matters more than the red mark.

Review closes the loop

A correction you never return to disappears quickly. A word heard once or a sentence said in a hurry disappears too. Review is what keeps the whole system from falling apart after the first week.

Spaced repetition means you return to a word or correction when you are about to forget it. Easy items come back later. Hard items come back sooner. You do not have to track the schedule yourself.

In Soliloquy, words from stories, corrections from speaking, and phrases you practice go into one deck. The app suggests what is worth reviewing today.

Build a small foundation

You do not need all of grammar to start. You need a few basics: pronouns, the present tense, negation, questions, the past tense, and simple linking phrases. That is enough to talk about yourself and your day.

Do not learn these things in isolation. Use each rule in a sentence right away. "No trabajo hoy" is better than a table of verb forms in a notebook.

Build vocabulary in small steps too. Start with the most common words and the words from your own life. Do not start with a list of a thousand words you will never use.

Listen, but not instead of speaking

Listening develops understanding and gives you models. It does not replace speaking. You can listen to a podcast for an hour and still not be able to say a sentence about yourself.

Choose short material at your level. First listen for meaning. Then notice the rhythm and pronunciation. Finally say the corrected sentence out loud. Listening supports speaking, but it does not do the speaking for you.

A beginner week

  • Day 1: Pick 3 words and say one sentence of your own with them. Write it down.
  • Day 2: Return to that sentence. Say it again and add a second one.
  • Day 3: Ask for one correction. Use a tutor, language exchange, or an app.
  • Day 4: Read a short text. Pick 3 new words and answer a question about your life out loud.
  • Day 5: Build a longer answer, about 5 sentences. Record it.
  • Day 6: Review your corrections and flashcards. Notice one pattern you keep fixing.
  • Day 7: Listen to your recordings from the week. Pick one thing to work on next.

This is a starting point. The whole thing fits in 10 to 15 minutes a day. On a busy day, do one speaking exercise and one review session.

What to ignore for now

  • Grammar terminology. You need some grammar, but you do not need to name every tense before you speak.
  • A perfect accent. Accent is part of who you are. The goal is to be understood.
  • A huge word list. Learn words you can use in your own sentences.
  • Listening as background noise. A podcast on the bus is not a study plan.
  • Comparing yourself to polyglots on social media. Their time and conditions are not yours.
  • A fixed date for fluency. No one can honestly promise a level by a date.

How to measure progress

Do not measure only the words that passed in front of your eyes. Measure what you can do:

  • Can you use a word from a story in your own sentence without looking at notes?
  • Can you say more about your day than you could a month ago?
  • Do you understand a correction the first time?
  • Does speaking out loud feel less scary than it did?

These signs are small, but they say more about your progress than a word count.

Hard questions

Do I need to learn grammar first?

No. Learn a small piece of grammar and use it in a sentence right away. Grammar makes sense when it helps you say something real.

How long does it take to speak comfortably?

No one can give you one honest date. It depends on your starting point, the language, how regularly you practice, and what you do in that practice. Daily practice gives you a chance to improve. A date in the calendar does not guarantee it.

Do I need a tutor?

Conversation with a tutor is the best way to practice real conversation, but you do not need one to start. A tutor helps most when you want to work on spontaneity and reacting in real time.

Is listening to podcasts enough?

No. Listening develops understanding and gives you models, but it does not teach speaking by itself. You need words you can use and sentences said out loud. Combine the two: listen to a short recording, take a few words from it, and answer with one sentence of your own.

Can I learn two languages at once?

You can, but it takes more time and slows progress in both. If you do it, keep the sessions separate and expect a slower pace.

Start with one loop

A good beginner strategy does not have to be complicated. Pick a few words, say one sentence of your own, ask for a correction, and return to it in review. Then repeat the loop.
